headline: Nvidia proposes $2,000 annual software fee per GPU for AI agent infrastructure
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang discussed a potential $2,000 annual license per GPU at GTC Berlin, a model that could generate $50 billion over five years if 5 million GPUs are covered.
details: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has discussed a potential annual software licensing cost of around $2,000 per GPU. This pricing model could generate $50 billion over five years under a scenario involving five million paid licenses, as outlined by FourWeekMBA.

Huang revealed this at GTC Berlin, emphasizing that software licensing will become a major part of Nvidia's business. The fee would cover "all the software that Nvidia provides that runs agents on these AI factories."

The company currently charges $4,500 per GPU for a one-year subscription to its AI Enterprise platform. It's unclear if the proposed $2,000 fee covers the same products or licensing terms, and Nvidia has not confirmed it as a standard price or a price cut.

This licensing discussion comes as Nvidia expands its infrastructure for deploying and managing AI agents in enterprise environments. These agents use tools, access data, and execute tasks, creating new security and management challenges.

To address this, Nvidia announced its OpenShell Reference Architecture, combining Vera Rubin computing infrastructure, Vera CPUs, and BlueField-4 DPUs running Nvidia Sentry. OpenShell provides a secure runtime for AI agents.

Sentry independently monitors agent activity and can quarantine agents attempting to breach boundaries. This architecture aims to integrate security controls directly into the underlying infrastructure, rather than relying solely on AI model safeguards.

Other companies are adopting these controls; Anthropic is integrating OpenShell with Claude Managed Agents, and Salesforce developed a Slack Admin Bridge for OpenShell. This allows businesses greater control and monitoring over AI agent actions.

The proposed software pricing aligns with Huang's vision of Nvidia evolving beyond just a GPU supplier. The company is expanding into networking, systems, enterprise software, and comprehensive AI workload infrastructure.

headline_marked: [[Devs Learning With AI Scored 17 Points Lower]] in Anthropic's Trial vs. Coding Solo
headline: Devs Learning With AI Scored 17 Points Lower in Anthropic's Trial vs. Coding Solo
summary: A new study by Anthropic found that junior developers using AI assistants to learn a new library scored 17 percentage points lower on a quiz compared to those who coded by hand, especially in debugging.
details: A randomized trial by Anthropic revealed that developers learning a new library with an AI assistant scored significantly lower on a subsequent quiz. The AI group averaged 50%, while the group coding by hand averaged 67%, a 17-percentage-point difference.

This substantial gap was primarily observed in debugging questions, indicating a potential impact on fundamental skill development. Interestingly, the speed difference between the two groups was minimal and not statistically significant.

The study involved 52 "mostly junior" software engineers, all of whom had over a year of weekly Python experience and had used AI coding assistants before. Participants were new to Trio, a Python library for async concurrency, making it a fresh learning experience.

Each participant was tasked with building two Trio features within 35 minutes: a timer and a record fetcher. Half of the participants were allowed to use an AI assistant during this task, while the other half worked without one, followed by a 14-question quiz.

While AI users encountered fewer errors during the coding task (median 1 error vs. 3 for hand coders), the authors suspect that these errors were crucial for learning. The AI group had a smoother experience but ultimately retained less knowledge.

Hand coders frequently encountered and resolved Trio-specific mistakes, such as RuntimeWarning for an unawaited coroutine. The process of figuring out why these errors occurred directly taught them core concepts like what a coroutine is.

Analysis of interaction patterns showed that using AI primarily for debugging led to the lowest quiz scores. Conversely, participants who used AI for conceptual inquiry (e.g., "what does a nursery do?") retained most of the learning with minimal time cost.

The findings suggest that the risk of reduced learning is highest when developers are new to the specific technology they are building. This is particularly relevant for junior developers who are constantly encountering new tools and concepts.

The study implies a staged approach to learning: juniors should first attempt unfamiliar code solo, then use an AI agent to explain concepts, and only later delegate coding tasks to the AI once foundational understanding is established.

Tools like Claude Code's "Learning" output style, which explains choices and leaves design decisions to the human, can support stage two. Integrated development environments like Hermes IDE also offer features for managing agent sessions and reviewing changes to facilitate these learning stages.
